articles.title: EU condemns elections to Russian State Duma in occupied Ukrainian territories
articles.body:
The European Union has condemned the holding of elections to the Russian State Duma in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, assuring that it will never recognize them, and that sanctions will be applied to those involved in their organization.
A corresponding statement by High Representative Kaja Kallas on behalf of the EU regarding the elections to the State Duma of Russia held on September 18-20, 2026, and their non-applicability on the territory of Ukraine, was distributed in Brussels on Monday.
The European Union strongly condemned the illegal organization by the Russian Federation of so-called "elections" in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, namely in the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol, as well as in parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson regions, stating that these votes represented another blatant violation by Russia of international law, in particular the UN Charter, as well as the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of Ukraine.
In this regard, the EU called on Russia to respect Ukraine's internationally recognized borders and sovereignty, reiterating that it does not and will never recognize either the holding of these so-called "elections" in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine or their results. It assured that sanctions would be applied to persons involved in organizing these fictitious elections or running as candidates in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, as well as to those responsible for undermining the possibility of holding free and fair elections in Russia itself.
In addition, the European Union reaffirmed its unwavering support for the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders, urging that Russia must stop its illegal war of aggression against Ukraine, agree to a full, immediate, and unconditional ceasefire, and immediately, completely, and unconditionally withdraw its troops and equipment from the entire territory of Ukraine.
Regarding the elections in Russia itself, the High Representative stated that they once again highlighted the ongoing and deep erosion of democracy in Russia, which is taking place in an increasingly authoritarian political environment, noting that the lack of a level playing field for all participants was further complicated by Russia's illegal war of aggression against Ukraine and the ongoing illegal occupation of Ukrainian territories.
The statement emphasized that the Russian authorities continue to step up systematic and institutionalized domestic and transnational repression to prevent any democratic opposition forces from participating in the struggle against the status quo, and that the decision to bar candidates from the Yabloko party from participating in the elections on the federal list further limited the choice for Russian voters by removing one of the last opposition forces and the only party with an anti-war program from the electoral process.
The text also pointed to such facts as the large-scale abuse of administrative and judicial resources to eliminate all those who opposed Russia's illegal war of aggression, deprive Russian voters of a real choice regarding the future of their country, and significantly limit Russians' access to independent information, adding that the European Union and its member states will continue to support the important work of Russian civil society organizations, human rights defenders, and independent media.
Furthermore, the EU expressed regret over Russian's decision not to invite OSCE observers to these elections, stating that this once again demonstrated Russian’s disregard for the commitments undertaken by all OSCE participating states and deprived Russian voters and institutions of the opportunity to receive an impartial and independent assessment of the elections.

Russian Drones Hit Homes, University and Shopping Center in Zaporizhzhia, Injuring Six
At least six civilians were injured in an overnight Russian drone attack on Zaporizhzhia that damaged residential buildings and civilian infrastructure, according to Mykhailo Semikin of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration on September 21.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian forces targeted residential areas and civilian facilities with drones, damaging several apartment buildings, a university, and a shopping center, Semikin said.
Six civilians were injured in the attack and are receiving necessary medical assistance.
Emergency crews worked at the sites of the strikes throughout the night to address the aftermath of the attack. Several fires caused by the strikes have already been extinguished, while response efforts remain ongoing.
Following the attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was continuing to escalate its actions and warned that Moscow was signaling its readiness to expand the war.
“Russia is not backing down from its escalation and is sending many signals that it is ready to expand the war. All of this is happening as the stability of the world has already been shattered by this war,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
The president added that pressure on Russia must continue in order to bring the war to an end, emphasizing that Ukraine’s retaliatory actions and long-range sanctions were proving effective.
“At the UN General Assembly, we will discuss how we can achieve peace through joint efforts. This is the main task that all leaders should be working on. I thank everyone who is helping,” Zelenskyy noted.
The attack on Zaporizhzhia came amid Russian strikes elsewhere in Ukraine. On September 18, Russian forces struck Sumy and surrounding areas with six to seven guided aerial bombs, killing two people and injuring at least five others, including a child.
One of the bombs hit a multi-story residential building in the city’s Kovpakivskyi district, striking between the third and fourth floors.

articles.body:
Iran’s economy contracts by more than 10% during US war, official data shows
TEHRAN - Iran’s economy contracted by more than 10 per cent during the Middle East war, which began with US-Israeli attacks in late February.
The country’s gross domestic product (GDP) shrank by 10.1 per cent year-on-year from late March to late June, a period known in Iran as the first quarter of the Persian calendar, according to the Statistical Center of Iran on Sept 20.
Iran has been at war with the United States since late February, when US-Israeli strikes killed the Islamic republic’s supreme leader and senior military officials at the start of a vast offensive.
The strikes sparked Tehran’s retaliation in blocking the Strait of Hormuz – causing global oil prices to surge – as the conflict spread in the Middle East.
Aside from this, Iran’s economy has long struggled with hyperinflation and devaluation of its currency, caused in large part by economic sanctions. AFP

articles.title: France and Slovakia's threat to scupper 3,000 EU sanctions to protect two Russian oligarchs gathers steam
articles.body:
EU sanctions U-turn: France and Slovakia force bloc to delist two Russian oligarchs
Editor's note: This is a developing story.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — France and Slovakia seem to have succeeded in their push to remove two Russian oligarchs from EU sanctions on the afternoon of Sept. 21, after weeks of delaying the renewal of the bloc's 3,000 sanctions on Russia.
In exchange, EU ambassadors have provisionally agreed to extend the sanctions for 36 months rather than the originally planned 12 months, three national diplomats told the Kyiv Independent.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha took to social media to slam the agreement.
"What has changed? Nothing. Delisting is unacceptable and would send the wrong signal to Moscow at a time when pressure needs to increase," Sybiha wrote.
The ambassadors are expected to meet in the evening — for the third time in a single day — to confirm they have reached an agreement.
The technical vote to roll over the sanctions was held hostage by France and Slovakia, who wanted to delist the oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman.
read also
Slovakia has held the position for some time, repeatedly demanding that the oligarchs be delisted, but France's decision to support the move came as a surprise to some.
Paris has joined the demand because it is allegedly being requested by Azerbaijan, which France told EU countries is holding two of its nationals as political prisoners.
After EU ambassadors hold their evening meeting, ministers from the 27 countries will vote to adopt the agreement — a formality — ahead of the Sept. 22 deadline to renew the sanctions.
Ukraine's sanctions envoy Vladyslav Vlasiuk voiced frustration on social media over the latest EU ambassadors' meeting, asking, "How can anyone seriously discuss sanctions delisting while Russia's war continues?"
"Delisting without a fundamental change in conduct sends exactly the wrong signal: pressure is temporary, accountability is negotiable, and sanctions can simply be waited out," Vlasiuk said.
And the new ambassador to the EU, Taras Kachka, said: "Compromise only invites Moscow to raise the stakes."
The two sanctioned individuals, Fridman and Usmanov, are both considered members of Russian leader Vladimir Putin's inner circle.
Fridman is a co-founder of the Russian conglomerate Alfa-Group, whose subsidiary provided insurance for vehicles used by Russian forces in Ukraine, and reportedly serviced the Main Office of Special Programs, which is responsible for guarding Putin.
The Ukrainian-born tycoon was also the owner of Sense Bank — formerly known as Alfa-Bank, one of Ukraine's largest banks — before its nationalization in 2023.
Usmanov made his fortune in metal and mining operations following the collapse of the Soviet Union. He was referred to as "one of Putin's favorite oligarchs" in the EU's original 2022 sanctions decision.

articles.title: India’s fertilizer sector hit by sulfur price surge
articles.body:
India’s fertilizer sector hit by sulfur price surge
India’s fertilizer industry is facing renewed pressure from soaring sulfur prices as attacks on energy infrastructure in Russia and the Middle East tighten supplies of a key raw material used in phosphate fertilizers. 
Landed sulfur prices in India have doubled since the start of the year to around $1,050-$1,100 per ton, raising costs for producers of diammonium phosphate (DAP), single super phosphate (SSP), and other complex fertilizers. 
India consumes around 3.8-3.9 million tons of sulfur annually, with more than half used by the fertilizer industry. Indian companies use sulfur and phosphate rock to manufacture fertilizers domestically. Sulfur availability is key for food security in the world’s most populous nation. 
Most sulfur is recovered as a byproduct of oil refining and natural gas processing rather than mined directly. It is then converted into sulfuric acid, which is used to process phosphate rock for fertilizers such as DAP and SSP. 
Ukraine doubled the number of Russian refineries targeted in the first five months of the year compared with the same period in last year, Reuters reported. Moscow has restricted exports of sulfur and sulfuric acid to protect supplies for its domestic fertilizer industry amid the disruptions. Sulfuric acid export restrictions are set to remain in place through the end of the year.
The Middle East conflict has added to the supply pressure. Nearly half of globally traded seaborne sulfur normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz, where shipments fell sharply during the Iran war before beginning to recover in June.
Higher demand from the battery industry has added to the squeeze, with sulfuric acid increasingly being used to process nickel for electric-vehicle battery materials, particularly in Indonesia.
Russia has pledged to increase fertilizer supplies to India. “We are doing everything to resolve this issue for Indian farmers and agriculture; we are increasing these supplies and are ready to continue doing so,” Russian President Vladimir Putin told Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar in Moscow earlier this month.

articles.title: Russia-Ukraine strikes kill two as Kiev urges renewed push for peace
articles.body:
At least two people were killed and 11 others injured in overnight strikes across Ukraine and a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Bryansk region, as Kiev called for greater international pressure to end the war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that Russia launched strikes across 10 Ukrainian regions overnight, killing one person and injuring eight others.
In a statement on X, Zelenskyy accused Moscow of sending signals that it was prepared to widen the conflict, saying Russia was “not backing down from its escalation.”
He said a Russian attack on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured five people and damaged nine-story residential buildings, a university facility, a shopping mall and a boiler house. Some residents were forced to evacuate, according to Zelenskyy.
In the Kharkiv region, a woman was killed in a drone strike and three other people were injured, he said.
Kiev calls for pressure and diplomacy
Zelenskyy said Ukraine would use the UN General Assembly’s high-level week in New York to discuss joint efforts toward peace.
“This is the main task that all leaders should be working on,” he said, calling for continued pressure on Russia through sanctions and other measures while stressing that diplomacy must proceed alongside such efforts.
“Every response and every long-range sanction is part of the pressure that is actually working,” Zelenskyy said.
Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its forces struck multiple targets in Ukraine, including two cargo vessels it said were being used for military purposes, a gas distribution station, infrastructure at the Izmail port and the BDU Logistic centre in Kiev region.
Deadly strike reported in Russia
In Russia, a man was killed and three people were injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Bryansk region, which borders Ukraine, acting regional governor Yegor Kovalchuk said on Monday.
The latest exchanges come as international diplomatic efforts continue to seek a path toward ending the Russia-Ukraine war, which has entered its fourth year.

articles.title: Corruption and Attitudes Toward People: Terekhov on the Key Tasks to Be Resolved as Part of the Reform of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers
articles.body:
Corruption and Attitudes Toward People: Terekhov on the Key Tasks to Be Resolved as Part of the Reform of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers
Kyiv • UNN
Terekhov identified cases of corruption among employees of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers as one of the problems negatively affecting society's attitude toward the mobilization process.
Reforming the territorial recruitment and social support centers is necessary, but so far there have been no tangible changes in their work. Ihor Terekhov, head of the Association of Frontline Cities and Communities, said this in an interview with RBC-Ukraine, reports UNN.
"At the beginning of the year, the president instructed the defense minister to reform the territorial recruitment and social support centers. Unfortunately, there has been no tangible progress so far, and reform is certainly needed," Terekhov said.
He described cases of corruption among territorial recruitment and social support center employees as one of the problems negatively affecting public attitudes toward the mobilization process.
"The first thing that concerns society is that some territorial recruitment and social support center officials are exposed taking bribes—they take money to release people, and then this gets into the information space, and there is no trust left. If these are isolated cases, that is one thing—a 'bad apple' can be found everywhere. But if it becomes a system, the attitude is completely different," said the head of the Association of Frontline Cities and Communities.
Terekhov named the attitude of territorial recruitment and social support center employees toward people as another issue that needs to be resolved as part of the reform. According to him, high-profile incidents during mobilization measures harm not only the recruitment and social support centers themselves but also trust in the Armed Forces.
"We have seen terrible cases; I commented on them, and people took to the streets because of this. This must be eliminated—it undermines trust in the Armed Forces," Terekhov emphasized.
He added that he had discussed this problem directly with military personnel stationed in the hottest areas of the front.
"I communicate with real servicemen who are fighting in the hottest areas of the front, and they say that such behavior destroys their image—they themselves despise such methods," the head of the Association of Frontline Cities and Communities concluded.

Ukrainian Drones Hunt Down Hidden Russian T-72 Tank and D-30 Howitzer
Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian T-72 tank and a D-30 howitzer in the Donbas region after detecting the equipment concealed in a wooded area, Ukraine’s 40th Separate Marine Brigade reported on September 21.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to footage released by the brigade, drone operators from its Orion Unmanned Systems Battalion identified the Russian armored vehicle and artillery system before carrying out precision strikes.
“Fighters of the Orion Unmanned Systems Battalion of the 40th Separate Marine Brigade destroyed an enemy T-72 tank and a D-30 gun. Our UAV operators in the Donbas detected enemy armored vehicles and carried out a precise strike,” the brigade said.
The latest strikes follow other recent Ukrainian drone operations targeting concealed Russian armored vehicles and equipment. On February 15, Ukrainian forces destroyed another Russian T-72 tank near the settlement of Yampil in a coordinated operation involving several military units.
The tank was initially disabled by a precision strike before Ukrainian forces launched a series of additional attacks to destroy the vehicle. Footage released by the Apachi Battalion of the 81st Separate Airmobile Slobozhanska Brigade showed a final drone carrying a napalm payload striking the immobilized tank and setting it ablaze, leaving the vehicle extensively burned.
In a separate operation, Ukrainian drone operators located and struck Russian armored vehicles concealed from aerial reconnaissance, destroying an infantry fighting vehicle hidden inside a hangar and damaging a tank, according to footage released by the Pentagon unmanned aviation battalion of the 225th Separate Assault Brigade.
The battalion said that difficult winter weather, including strong winds, precipitation, and poor visibility, had complicated aerial reconnaissance along the frontline. Despite those conditions, the unit said its drone operations continued at full intensity.
